cells.tense: The hands are on the work now, and the work is answering back.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: Surfacing from the work, ask whoever's nearby how it's going for them — and when they answer, give them your whole attention before you go back.
cells.core:
You've built something that holds, and you built it the slow way. Same motion, most days, until your hands know it without you. That's not stubbornness — it's how skill gets made. Small and steady, and it stays.

Here's what the quiet can cost. The bench is easy to mistake for the whole world. So once, surfacing from the work, turn to someone nearby and ask how it's going for them. Then give them your whole attention while they answer. Don't fix anything, don't relate it back to the work — just let what they feel be theirs while you're both there. You build alone by design. You don't have to be alone in it.
cells.sheetLine: You built it slow, and now it holds without you watching.
cells.verb: laying down the work piece by piece until it holds
cells.place: at the bench where the same motion is repeated until it turns to skill

cells.tense: The next stage of the practice is being rehearsed in the head before the hands have done today's work.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: Before adding another layer, name what the practice costs someone close to you — then make the call yourself, fair or not, and say which it is.
cells.core:
You're running the practice ahead of itself. The hands haven't finished today's set and the head is already pricing tomorrow's, the week after, the year — planning past what any of it can show you yet. The discipline that built something real is now bracing against a future it can't write in.

Before you add one more layer, stop and count what the practice is taking from someone close to you. Not how it feels about them — what it actually costs them. Then make that call yourself: fair or not. If it's fair, say so out loud and carry it. If it isn't, that's information, and the next layer can wait. Weighing it is the point. Feeling bad about it instead isn't the same as weighing it.

cells.tense: The practice has stopped, and the bench is kept ready as if it might start again on its own.
cells.act: drop one condition you set and take the step
cells.ask: Name the condition you've attached to starting again — the right hour, the right setup, the right mood — and set it down. Then step in anyway.
cells.core:
The bench is still set up like nothing happened. You know how to build — the hands remember — but nothing's being made. What's left is the equipment and the intention, and the intention isn't moving.

One condition is doing this. You've set a bar for starting again — the right stretch of time, the right gear, being in the right frame with it — and that bar is a demand for a clean run, not a plan. Name it. Put it down. Then step in anyway: ten minutes, bad form, counting for nothing. That's not the practice coming back. It's the door you're standing behind being opened.

cells.tense: You are doing this daily and describing it as nothing much, in the voice you'd use about the weather.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin something at this bench only because you want to try it — no goal, no use for it yet — and say nothing about it to anyone.
cells.core:
You do this most days, and you'd tell it flat if anyone asked — just keeping your hand in. Meanwhile the thing you've built is holding people up, quietly, because you keep showing up to the same bench and doing the same motion until it's right. The discipline is real work. You talk about it like it's worth nothing.

Before this was upkeep, it began as something you wanted to try. So begin something at the bench with no goal yet — a first attempt at something that just interests you — and say nothing about it to anyone. Nothing depends on it and nothing's grading it. The itch to try a thing got buried under the doing. It's still yours to pick up.
